Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $c>0$ be a fixed real constant.
All curves below take values in $M$; the physical reading of $c$, of a
worldline as the history of a clock or body, and of the parameter values as
times is not part of this definition and is adopted separately in the
postulates of the framework.

**(a) Regularity classes.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A
**chart representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ for a smooth
chart $(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]).

- For $k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ and an interior point $t_0\in I$, the map
  $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ at $t_0$** when there is a chart representative
  $x\circ\gamma$ defined near $t_0$ that is $C^k$ there in the componentwise
  Euclidean sense. This condition is independent of the chart: on the overlap
  of two chart representatives the transition map is smooth and the chain rule
  applies ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]],
  [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). If $t_0\in I$ is an
  included endpoint of $I$, the coordinate representative and its derivatives through order $k$
  are continuous up to $t_0$ on the relative interval
  $I\cap(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$, with derivatives at
  $t_0$ taken one-sided. For $k=\infty$ this holds at every finite order.
  Merely possessing a one-sided secant tangent, as defined next, does not
  by itself make a curve $C^1$ at the endpoint. The map $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ on $I$** when it is $C^k$ at
  every point of $I$.

- Let $b\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. A curve
  $\gamma:(b-\varepsilon,b]\to M$ has **left tangent** $v\in T_{\gamma(b)}M$
  at $b$ when for one — equivalently every — chart $(U,x)$ around
  $\gamma(b)$, writing $v=\sum_{a=0}^{3}v^a\partial_a|_{\gamma(b)}$
  ([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the
  difference quotients satisfy
  $\bigl(x^a(\gamma(t))-x^a(\gamma(b))\bigr)/(t-b)\to v^a$ as $t\uparrow b$ for
  $a=0,1,2,3$. A **right tangent** at the left end of a curve is defined
  analogously with $t\downarrow b$. Chart independence is the one-sided
  chain-rule computation for the smooth transition maps
  ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

- A curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ is **piecewise $C^1$** when there is a
  finite partition $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ such that for every $i$ the
  restriction of $\gamma$ to $[s_{i-1},s_i]$ is $C^1$ up to its included
  endpoints in the one-sided sense above: in every endpoint chart its
  component derivatives on the open piece have continuous one-sided limits,
  agreeing with its endpoint derivatives. Equivalently each piece has a
  $C^1$ extension to its closed parameter piece. In particular its right
  tangent at $s_{i-1}$ and left tangent at $s_i$ exist. Such a
  partition is called **admissible** for $\gamma$. The piece extensions give continuity at the
  corners; no agreement of the
  two one-sided tangents at a corner is required.

**(b) Velocity.** If $\gamma$ is $C^1$ at an interior point $t$, its
**velocity** $\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation
$[f]\mapsto(f\circ\gamma)'(t)$ on smooth germs at $\gamma(t)$, extending
[[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]] from smooth to $C^1$ curves.
Equal germ representatives agree along the curve near $t$, and the
one-variable product rule proves the derivation identity. In a chart around
$\gamma(t)$ the velocity has the component
expression

$$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x^a\circ\gamma\bigr)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)},$$

the coordinate expression of the derivation
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). At an
included endpoint of the domain, $\gamma'$ means the corresponding one-sided
tangent of clause (a).

**(c) Timelike worldlines.** For $k\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$,
a **$C^k$ future timelike worldline** is a $C^k$
curve $\gamma:I\to M$ whose velocity $\gamma'(t)$ is future timelike at every
$t\in I$, in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]
and [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))<0$
and $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),N_{\gamma(t)})<0$. A **piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike worldline** is a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ whose
velocity at every point of each open piece and whose one-sided tangents at the
two ends of each piece are future timelike; the definition is applied to a map
on an arbitrary interval $I$ with nonempty interior by requiring it on every
compact subinterval of $I$. A future timelike velocity is in particular
nonzero, so every future timelike worldline is regular.

**(d) Proper time and length.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$
future timelike worldline and let $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ be an admissible
partition. On each open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the function

$$h_i(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}\bigl(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s)\bigr)}$$

is continuous and strictly positive: it is a finite sum of products of
continuous real functions in any chart around a point of the piece, as
$g_{ab}\circ\gamma$ and the components of $\gamma'$ are continuous
([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and the
square root is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ ([[def-rational-power]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The continuous one-sided limits of the component derivatives, required
by the $C^1$ extension of each piece, and continuity of $g$ imply that
$h_i$ tends to the norm of the corresponding endpoint tangent. The future
timelike hypothesis on those tangents makes these limits strictly positive, and $h_i$ extends to a continuous function on
$[s_{i-1},s_i]$; hence it is Darboux integrable there
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). The
**proper-time increment** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is

$$\tau(b)-\tau(a):=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h_i(s)\,ds,$$

and the **Lorentzian length** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is
$L_g(\gamma):=c\,(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. For a base point $s_0\in I$ the
**proper-time function** $\tau:I\to\mathbb R$ of a future timelike worldline is
the function with $\tau(s_0)=0$ and $\tau(s)$ equal to the increment
from $s_0$ to $s$ when $s>s_0$, and minus the increment from $s$ to $s_0$
when $s<s_0$. That the increment is independent of the admissible
partition, so that $\tau$ is well defined, and that it is invariant under
increasing $C^1$ reparametrization are proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]; the display is the
value for any admissible partition.

**(e) Four-velocity.** Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike
worldline and let $t$ be a parameter value at which $\gamma$ is differentiable
(interior point of a piece, or an included endpoint with its one-sided
tangent). The **four-velocity** of $\gamma$ at $t$ is

$$U(t):=\frac{c\,\gamma'(t)}{\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M .$$

By construction $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$, and
$\gamma'(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}/c\bigr)U(t)$ with a strictly
positive scalar factor. If $U$ is written as the derivative of $\gamma$ with
respect to proper time, $U=d\gamma/d\tau$, this is a statement proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]], not part of the
present definition.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.
If $(U,x)$ is a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$ with $p\in U$, then the coordinate derivations $\partial_1|_p,\dots,\partial_n|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). The **integral function of $f$ with base point $a$**
is

$$F : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_a^x f .$$

**It is a genuine function, and that has to be checked.** For $x \in (a,b]$ the
restriction of $f$ to $[a,x]$ is integrable, by
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] applied with $c := a$ and $d := x$, so
$\int_a^x f$ names a single real number ([[def-darboux-integral]]). For $x = a$
the symbol $\int_a^a f$ is $0$ by [[def-oriented-integral]]. So $F(x)$ is defined
at every point of $[a,b]$ and

$$F(a) \;=\; 0 .$$

More generally, for any base point $c \in [a,b]$ the function
$x \mapsto \int_c^x f$ is defined on the whole of $[a,b]$, the integral being the
oriented one of [[def-oriented-integral]] when $x < c$; the case $c = a$ is
written $F$ above and is the one used unless another base point is named.

### The two identities used throughout

**Increments are integrals.** For all $x, y \in [a,b]$, in either order,

$$F(y) - F(x) \;=\; \int_x^y f .$$

This is claim 3 of [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] applied to the three
points $a$, $x$, $y$: it gives $\int_a^x f + \int_x^y f = \int_a^y f$, that is
$F(x) + \int_x^y f = F(y)$. No ordering of $x$ and $y$ is assumed, and the
degenerate cases $x = y$, $x = a$ and $y = a$ are included, since claim 3 is
stated for arbitrary points.

**Changing the base point changes $F$ by a constant.** If $c \in [a,b]$ and
$F_c(x) := \int_c^x f$, then for every $x \in [a,b]$

$$F_c(x) \;=\; F(x) - F(c) ,$$

again by claim 3 of [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] at the points $a$, $c$,
$x$. So the family of integral functions of $f$ is one function up to an
additive constant.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $\phi:[c,d]\to[a,b]$ be a monotone surjection, differentiable on $[c,d]$ in the one-sided endpoint sense, with Riemann-integrable derivative. For every bounded $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$,
$$f\text{ is Riemann integrable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(f\circ\phi)|\phi'|\text{ is Riemann integrable},$$
and, when these conditions hold,
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\int_c^d f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt.$$
Flat subintervals of $\phi$ are allowed.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g(A) \subseteq B$, and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$. If $g$ is continuous
at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c) \in B$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then
$f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$.

**No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition
theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of
two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a
punctured neighbourhood of $c$; with both dropped the statement is false, which
is [[fs-naive-composition-of-limits]]. The first of those conditions is exactly
*continuity of $f$ at $L$* written out, so under the hypotheses above it holds
automatically and nothing has to be assumed. The mechanism is visible in the
proof: [[def-continuity-real]] quantifies over $|y - b| < \rho$ rather than over
$0 < |y - b| < \rho$, so the value $y = b$ that the limit version cannot control
is precisely the one the continuity hypothesis does control.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

derivations.claim: (Common refinement.) Let $P=\{s_i\}$ and $P'=\{s'_j\}$ be admissible partitions of $[a,b]$ for $\gamma$, and let $Q$ be the partition whose nodes are the union of the two node sets, ordered increasingly. Then $Q$ is an admissible partition: each interval of $Q$ lies in an interval of $P$ and in one of $P'$, hence inside one open piece of each of the two parametrizations, and $\gamma$ is $C^1$ there.

(The density is independent of the partition.) Define, for each interval $[u,v]$ contained in the closure of one open piece of $\gamma$, the number $H(u,v):=\int_u^v h$, where $h$ is the continuous positive extension of the density to $[u,v]$ from [L1]; this is the Darboux integral of a continuous function ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). If the nodes of a subpartition are inserted, [L3] gives additivity: $H(u,v)=H(u,w)+H(w,v)$.

(Strict positivity.) For $a<b$, choose an open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and a closed interval $[u,v]\subseteq(s_{i-1},s_i)$ with $u<v$. Fix the midpoint $t_*=(u+v)/2$. By continuity and $h(t_*)>0$, shrink the interval symmetrically about $t_*$ so that $h\ge m:=h(t_*)/2>0$ on the resulting $[u,v]$; every lower Darboux sum of $h$ on any partition refining $\{u,v\}$ is at least $m(v-u)$, since $h\ge m$ on $[u,v]$ and $h>0$ elsewhere. Hence the lower integral, which equals the integral because $h$ is integrable, is at least $m(v-u)>0$ ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]). Dividing by $c>0$ gives $\tau(b)-\tau(a)>0$ when $a<b$.

(Reparametrization: reduction to pieces.) By [L7], the continuous nowhere-zero derivative of $\varphi$ has one strict sign; consider first $\varphi'>0$. The mean value theorem makes $\varphi$ strictly increasing, and continuity makes its image exactly $[\alpha,\beta]$ with $\alpha=\varphi(a')<\beta=\varphi(b')$. Strict monotonicity gives continuity of its inverse: at each image value the images of nearby parameter endpoints bound a relative neighbourhood. Restrict $\gamma$ to $[\alpha,\beta]$ and let $P=\{s_i\}$ be an admissible partition of that restriction; the preimages $\varphi^{-1}(s_i)$ form an admissible partition for $\tilde\gamma=\gamma\circ\varphi$: on each preimage interval $(u,v)=\varphi^{-1}(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the curve $\tilde\gamma$ is the composition of $C^1$ maps and hence $C^1$, with $\tilde\gamma'=\varphi'\cdot(\gamma'\circ\varphi)$ by [L7], a strictly positive multiple of a future timelike vector and therefore future timelike by [L2].

(Derivative of the proper-time function.) Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a $C^1$ future timelike worldline and $\tau(t)=\frac1c\int_{t_0}^{t}h$ its proper-time function, $h$ continuous and positive on $I$. For each compact $[u,v]\subseteq I$, [L4] gives $\tau(v)-\tau(u)=\frac1c\int_u^vh$; since $h/c$ is continuous at every $t\in I$, the first fundamental theorem in the form $\tau'(t)=h(t)/c$ follows at every interior point, and one-sided at the endpoints. This is the displayed formula; it is $>0$ because $h>0$ and $c>0$.

(Partition independence.) Write the sum of the definition for $P$ as $\sum_iH(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and similarly for $P'$ and $Q$. Refining $P$ to $Q$ and applying additivity of step 1.2 to each interval of $P$ split by the nodes of $Q$, the sum for $P$ equals the sum over $Q$; the same holds for $P'$. Hence both sums equal $\sum_{Q}H$ and the increment is independent of the admissible partition.

(Reparametrization: the integral identity.) On a piece $(u,v)$ as in step 1.4, the density of $\tilde\gamma$ equals $\varphi'\cdot\sqrt{-g(\gamma'\circ\varphi,\gamma'\circ\varphi)} =\varphi'\,(h\circ\varphi)$ by bilinearity of the metric and $\varphi'>0$; it is continuous and positive on the closed piece. By [L5], $\int_u^v\varphi'\,(h\circ\varphi)=\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h$. Summing over the finitely many pieces and dividing by $c$ gives $\tilde\tau(b')-\tilde\tau(a')=\tau(\beta)-\tau(\alpha)$. At a piece endpoint the one-sided tangent of $\tilde\gamma$ is $\varphi'\gamma'$ with the same one-sided value of $\varphi'>0$, hence future timelike, so $\tilde\gamma$ is a future timelike worldline.

(Four-velocity relation.) At every $t\in I$, by the definition of $U$ and step 1.5, $\tau'(t)U(t)=\frac{h(t)}{c}\cdot\frac{c\gamma'(t)}{h(t)}=\gamma'(t)$ and $g(U(t),U(t))=\frac{c^2\,g(\gamma',\gamma')}{h(t)^2} =\frac{c^2g(\gamma',\gamma')}{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}=-c^2$. The same computation applies on each open piece and, by the continuous one-sided velocity and density extensions, at each included one-sided endpoint of a piecewise-$C^1$ worldline; a corner retains its two separate values.

(Reparametrization by proper time.) By step 1.5, $\tau$ is $C^1$, and its increments are strictly positive by step 1.3, so it is strictly increasing on $I$; let $J:=\tau(I)$ and $\psi:=\tau^{-1}:J\to I$. At each interior $\sigma\in J$, [L7] applied to $\tau$ at $t=\psi(\sigma)$ gives a $C^1$ local inverse; injectivity identifies it with $\psi$. At an included endpoint, monotonicity first gives continuity of the inverse from that side: any relative neighbourhood of $t$ has a strictly separated inner endpoint value under $\tau$. For $\sigma'\to\sigma$ from that side, put $t'=\psi(\sigma')$; then $t'\to t$ and $(\psi(\sigma')-\psi(\sigma))/(\sigma'-\sigma)=(t'-t)/(\tau(t')-\tau(t))\to1/\tau'(t)$. Continuity of $\tau'>0$ makes the inverse derivative continuous up to that endpoint. Applying the same local inverse and endpoint reciprocal-quotient argument to $\varphi$, whose derivative is continuous and nowhere zero, also proves the $C^1$ diffeomorphism-onto-image assertion in claim 2. Thus $\psi$ is $C^1$ on $J$ in the stated one-sided sense and $\psi'(\sigma)=1/\tau'(\psi(\sigma))$.

(Additivity over a splitting.) Fix any $u\in(a,b)$ and insert $u$ into an admissible partition, giving nodes $q_0=a<\cdots<q_j=u<\cdots<q_n=b$. By step 1.2 the total sum is $\sum_{i=1}^{j}H(q_{i-1},q_i)+\sum_{i=j+1}^{n}H(q_{i-1},q_i)$; after division by the fixed constant $c$, step 2.1 identifies these sums with the two subinterval increments. Thus $\tau(b)-\tau(a)=(\tau(u)-\tau(a))+(\tau(b)-\tau(u))$ for every such $u$.

(Reversing orientation.) For $\varphi'<0$, use its image $[\alpha,\beta]=[\varphi(b'),\varphi(a')]$; the chain rule gives $\tilde\gamma'=\varphi'(\gamma'\circ\varphi)$, a negative multiple of a future timelike tangent, hence past timelike. The closed-piece $C^1$ extensions compose in the same way, including their distinct corner values. Bilinearity gives $\tilde h=|\varphi'|(h\circ\varphi)$. Apply [L5] to the reversed endpoints on each piece and sum to get $\int_{a'}^{b'}\tilde h=\int_\alpha^\beta h>0$. Meanwhile the signed original difference is $\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a'))=\tau(\alpha)-\tau(\beta)<0$. If the image is the full interval $[a,b]$, this is $-(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. Thus the unsigned integral and oriented difference have different signs, as asserted; no proper-time function for a future curve is assigned a negative elapsed value.

(Velocity of the reparametrized curve.) For $\gamma_\tau=\gamma\circ\psi$ and $\sigma\in J$, [L7] applied in a chart around $\gamma(\psi(\sigma))$ gives $\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)=\psi'(\sigma)\,\gamma'(\psi(\sigma)) =\gamma'\bigl(\psi(\sigma)\bigr)/\tau'\bigl(\psi(\sigma)\bigr) =U(\psi(\sigma))$ by step 2.3. In particular $g(\gamma_\tau',\gamma_\tau')=-c^2$ and $\gamma_\tau'$ is future timelike, so $\gamma_\tau$ is a $C^1$ future timelike worldline on $J$; for a piecewise $C^1$ worldline the same construction applies on each closed piece using its one-sided inverse derivatives, with separate left and right velocities at a corner.

boundaries.reason: No union, product or indexed aggregate is quantified in the Statement; every claim is about one fixed worldline and finitely many explicitly constructed partitions of its parameter interval.

boundaries.evidence: Definition requires c>0 and a positive norm density on each closed piece; step 1.3 gives a positive lower bound on a small subinterval by continuity at its fixed midpoint. No normalization denominator vanishes.

citations.quote:
An **affine connection** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a connection on the tangent bundle $TM$ in the sense of [[def-connection-on-a-smooth-vector-bundle]]. Thus it assigns a vector field $
abla_XY$ to two vector fields and is function-linear in the differentiating direction $X$, real-linear in $Y$, and obeys $
abla_X(fY)=X(f)Y+f
abla_XY$.

The word affine imposes neither a metric nor torsion freeness. The tangent-bundle specialization allows the Lie bracket of $X,Y$ to be compared with their covariant derivatives; there is no corresponding bracket on sections of a general vector bundle. Manifolds with boundary are allowed, and tangent vectors at their boundary need not be tangent to the boundary. The empty and zero-dimensional manifolds have the unique tangent-bundle connection.

For an affine connection, define its **torsion** on local vector fields by
$$T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y].$$
The connection is as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]], and the bracket is the smooth vector field given by [[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket]]. The next lemma proves this operation is a smooth alternating tangent-valued two-tensor. It is called **torsion free** when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all local fields.

This construction uses the tangent bundle: general bundle sections have no Lie bracket with which to form this difference. In dimension zero all terms vanish. Smooth fields on a manifold with boundary need not be boundary-tangent; bracket and covariant derivative use smooth coordinate derivatives there as well.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. Then $f\mapsto Xf$ is an
$\mathbb R$-linear derivation of $C^\infty(M)$:

$$ X(fg)=f\,Xg+g\,Xf $$

for all $f,g\in C^\infty(M)$.

For smooth vector fields $X,Y$ and smooth functions $f,g$ on $M$,

$$ [X,fY]=f[X,Y]+(Xf)Y $$

and

$$ [fX,gY]=fg[X,Y]+f(Xg)Y-g(Yf)X. $$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be smooth vector fields on $M$. Their **Lie bracket** is the
operator on smooth functions defined by

$$ [X,Y]f:=X(Yf)-Y(Xf). $$

The next results show that this commutator is again induced by a smooth vector
field on $M$.

In a chart $(U,x^1,\dots,x^n)$, if

$$ X=\sum_{i=1}^n X^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}, \qquad Y=\sum_{i=1}^n Y^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}, $$

then on $U$

$$ [X,Y]=\sum_{j=1}^n \left(\sum_{i=1}^n X^i\partial_iY^j-Y^i\partial_iX^j\right)\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}. $$

Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$, and let $X$ be a vector
field on $U$. Then $X$ is smooth if and only if there exist smooth functions
$X^1,\dots,X^n:U\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$ X=\sum_{i=1}^n X^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} $$

on $U$.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), with smooth atlas
$\mathcal A$ and maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$
([[def-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]). For $p\in M$ the
tangent space $T_pM$ is the real vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]), and the cotangent space is its
algebraic dual $T_p^*M:=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]).

A **covariant $2$-tensor at $p$** is a bilinear map
$A_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$. It is **symmetric** when
$A_p(v,w)=A_p(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in T_pM$, and **nondegenerate** when the only
$v\in T_pM$ with $A_p(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in T_pM$ is $v=0$.

A **smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$** is a family $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor $A_p$ at $p$, such that for every
chart $(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$ the **component
functions**

$$A_{ab}(q):=A_q\!\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^a}\Big|_q,\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^b}\Big|_q\right),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$. Here $\partial/\partial x^a|_q$ is the coordinate
derivation at $q$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the index
ranges over the label set $I_n=\{1,\dots,n\}$ (or the relabelled set
$I_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ when $n=4$), and smoothness of the real-valued functions
$A_{ab}$ on the open set $U\subseteq M$ is the notion of
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] applied to $M$ and
$\mathbb R$.

For a coordinate tuple $z\in x(U)$ define the **coordinate representative**
$A^x_{ab}(z):=A_{ab}(x^{-1}(z))$. When the argument is a coordinate tuple,
$A_{ab}(z)$ abbreviates this representative in the named chart; when it is a
point of $M$, it denotes the component function on the chart domain. Thus
$A_{ab}(x(y^{-1}(u)))$ in a change-of-coordinates formula means
$A^x_{ab}((x\circ y^{-1})(u))$, never evaluation of a function on $M$ at a
tuple. For $n=4$, $x^a$ and $\partial_a$ mean the original coordinate and
derivation labelled $a+1$, respectively; this relabels every slot and sum.
The label $0$ alone gives no coordinate vector a causal character.

Because the coordinate derivations at $q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), specifying
$A$ is the same as specifying the matrix of component functions in each chart;
[[lem-gr-covariant-two-tensor-transformation-law]] proves that the smoothness
requirement is independent of the chart used, so that the condition may be
checked on any smooth atlas of $M$, and derives the transformation law relating
components in two overlapping charts.

The field is **symmetric** when $A_p$ is symmetric for every $p\in M$, which in
a chart is the identity $A_{ab}=A_{ba}$ of component functions; it is
**nondegenerate** when $A_p$ is nondegenerate for every $p$, which in a chart is
the nonvanishing at every point of the polynomial function
$\det(A_{ab})$ of the components. The **matrix** of $A$ in a chart means the
matrix $\bigl(A_{ab}(q)\bigr)$ of its component functions at $q$.

**Convention.** In the four-dimensional case $n=4$ used in this library, indices
are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ with $0$ the time-coordinate label when such a coordinate is chosen, and we write
$A_{ab}$ for the components. A covariant $2$-tensor field is also called a
**$(0,2)$ tensor field**.
If $(U,x)$ is a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$ with $p\in U$, then the coordinate derivations $\partial_1|_p,\dots,\partial_n|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$.

Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$, and let $X$ be a vector
field on $U$. Then $X$ is smooth if and only if there exist smooth functions
$X^1,\dots,X^n:U\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$ X=\sum_{i=1}^n X^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} $$

on $U$.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.
Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $r\in\mathbb N$. If the entries of $A:U\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ are $C^r$ and $\det A$ never vanishes, then the entries of $A^{-1}$ are $C^r$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $\nabla$ be an affine connection on
$M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) and let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, with Christoffel symbols $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a
\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]])
and metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$. Then:

1. $\nabla$ is torsion-free ([[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]])
   if and only if $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\Gamma^a{}_{cb}$ for all $a,b,c$ in every
   smooth chart.
2. $\nabla$ is $g$-compatible ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) if and
   only if, in every smooth chart,

$$\partial_ag_{bc}=\sum_{d=0}^{3}\bigl(\Gamma^d{}_{ab}g_{dc}+\Gamma^d{}_{ac}g_{bd}\bigr) \qquad(a,b,c=0,1,2,3).$$

Thus $\nabla$ is metric-selected for $(M,g)$ if and only if both displayed
conditions hold in every smooth chart.

The **dual connection** on the smooth bundle $E^*$ of [[def-connection-on-a-smooth-vector-bundle]] is characterized by
$$ (\nabla^*_X\alpha)(s)=X(\alpha(s))-\alpha(\nabla_Xs).$$
The right side is function-linear in $s$: replacing $s$ by $fs$ introduces $X(f)\alpha(s)$ once with each sign, so those terms cancel.

Here is the construction, including well-definedness. In a frame $e$ write $s=eu$ and write $\alpha$ with dual coefficient column $a$, so $\alpha(s)=a^Tu$. The coordinate formula [[prop-local-coordinate-formula-for-a-bundle-connection]] gives
$$X(a^Tu)-a^T(X(u)+\omega(X)u)=(X(a)-\omega(X)^Ta)^Tu.$$
Thus the required coefficients are $X(a)-\omega(X)^Ta$, and the local connection matrix in the dual frame is $-\omega^T$. These local rules are smooth, real-linear and obey the section Leibniz rule by the scalar product rule. On an overlap both give the intrinsic displayed pairing formula; agreement against every local frame section forces equality of the dual covectors. They therefore glue to a connection, equivalently by [[thm-local-connection-forms-glue-exactly-when-they-obey-the-transformation-law]]. Testing against a basis also proves uniqueness. This verifies the implicit characterization rather than assuming that it defines an operator.

The derivative on scalar functions is $X(f)$; duality preserves the evaluation pairing with that scalar connection. For rank one the matrix changes sign; for rank zero evaluation and all coefficients are empty. Zero sections give zero derivatives, while empty bases give the unique operator. This construction is local and canonical from the given connection and requires no choice axiom.

Give each of finitely many bundles $E_j$ a connection. Use the tensor bundle constructed in [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]], including its multilinear model on the dual fibres. The **product connection** is characterized on local elementary tensors by
$$\nabla_X(s_1\otimes\cdots\otimes s_k)=\sum_j s_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\nabla^j_Xs_j\otimes\cdots\otimes s_k.$$
For the empty product, the connection on scalar functions is $\nabla_Xf=X(f)$.

To construct it without a decomposition assumption, for a multilinear-model section $T$ and local dual sections $\alpha_j$ put
$$(\nabla_XT)(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)=X\bigl(T(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)\bigr)-\sum_jT(\alpha_1,\ldots,(\nabla^j)^*_X\alpha_j,\ldots,\alpha_k).$$
Use the dual connections of [[def-dual-connection]]. Multiplying any argument by a smooth $f$ produces two opposite $X(f)T(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ terms; thus this expression is function-linear in every dual argument. In dual frames its coefficients are smooth and depend only on their fibre values, so it defines a smooth tensor section. The same intrinsic expression on overlaps gives agreement. Its real-linearity, function-linearity in $X$, and rule $\nabla_X(fT)=X(f)T+f\nabla_XT$ follow by direct expansion, establishing the connection. This also gives the gluing criterion of [[thm-local-connection-forms-glue-exactly-when-they-obey-the-transformation-law]].

On a pure tensor, the scalar product rule and the dual pairing identity reduce this expression to the first displayed sum. Hence it respects the balanced identity $(fs)\otimes t=s\otimes(ft)$: either derivative gives the same term $X(f)s\otimes t$ and the same two terms multiplied by $f$. Every section has a finite local product-frame expansion, so that rule and the connection Leibniz identity force uniqueness.

For bundles $E,F$, identify $F\otimes E^*$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(E,F)$ by $t\otimes\alpha\mapsto(v\mapsto\alpha(v)t)$. In local bases these elementary tensors are precisely the matrix units, proving this is a smooth fibrewise isomorphism. The induced **Hom connection** is therefore
$$(\nabla_XA)(s)=\nabla^F_X(A(s))-A(\nabla^E_Xs).$$
The two $X(f)A(s)$ terms cancel when $s$ is replaced by $fs$, ensuring a fibrewise map. Rank-zero factors give zero bundles, whereas the empty product is the scalar line; these conventions are different. No choice beyond finitely many local frames is needed.

For finite-rank smooth real vector bundles $E_1,\ldots,E_k$ on $M$, define the fibre tensor product to be the vector space of multilinear maps $E_{1,p}^*\times\cdots\times E_{k,p}^*\to\mathbb R$. The elementary tensor $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_k$ evaluates to $\prod_j\alpha_j(v_j)$. These spaces form a canonical smooth bundle, denoted $E_1\otimes\cdots\otimes E_k$, with product frames. Every local section is a finite sum of product-frame tensors with smooth coefficients. The empty product is the trivial real line.

Let $T$ be a type $(r,s)$ tensor on $V$ with $r,s\ge 1$. Contracting the first
contravariant slot against the first covariant slot gives the type
$(r-1,s-1)$ tensor $\operatorname{ctr}(T)$ defined intrinsically by

$$ \operatorname{ctr}(T)(\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_r,v_2,\ldots,v_s) :=\sum_i T(e^i,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_r,e_i,v_2,\ldots,v_s), $$

where $(e_i)$ is any basis of $V$ and $(e^i)$ its dual basis. The next lemma
shows that this formula is basis-independent.

derivations.claim: The functional $K$ is additive in each of its three arguments, and expanding its six terms with [L2] gives the three scalar rules $$K(fX,Y,Z)=fK(X,Y,Z),\qquad K(X,Y,fZ)=fK(X,Y,Z),$$ $$K(X,fY,Z)=fK(X,Y,Z)+2X(f)g(Y,Z)$$ for every smooth function $f$: in the first, the terms containing $Y(f)$ and $Z(f)$ produced by $[fX,Y]$ and $[fZ,X]$ cancel against the derivative-of-$f$ terms in $Y(g(Z,fX))$ and $-Z(g(fX,Y))$; in the second, the derivative terms cancel in pairs by symmetry of $g$; in the third, the terms $X(f)g(Y,Z)$ occur twice and all other derivative terms cancel.

Work with smooth local fields on each open chart domain and its overlaps. For fixed smooth $X,Y$, the rule of step 1.1 and bilinearity of $g$ show that the equation $2g(V,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for all smooth $Z$ is equivalent, in a chart, to the single set of identities $2g(V,\partial_c)=K(X,Y,\partial_c)$ for $c=0,1,2,3$: writing $Z=\sum_cZ^c\partial_c$ on the chart gives $K(X,Y,Z)=\sum_cZ^cK(X,Y,\partial_c)$.

In each smooth chart $(U,x)$ put $V_U:=\tfrac12\sum_{a,b}g^{ab}K(X,Y,\partial_b)\,\partial_a$, a smooth field on $U$; by step 2.1 and $g_{ac}g^{ab}=\delta_c{}^b$ it satisfies $2g(V_U,\partial_c)=2\sum_bg_{ac}g^{ab}\tfrac12K(X,Y,\partial_b)=K(X,Y,\partial_c)$ for every $c$, hence $2g(V_U,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth $Z$ on $U$. If $(U,x)$ and $(U',x')$ overlap, then $g(V_U-V_{U'},Z)=0$ for every smooth $Z$ there, so $V_U=V_{U'}$ pointwise by nondegeneracy; the local fields therefore patch to one smooth vector field $\nabla_XY$ on $M$ with $2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for all $Z$.

$
abla$ is an affine connection. Additivity and real homogeneity in $X$ and in $Y$ hold termwise for $K$; scalar linearity in $X$ is $K(fX,Y,Z)=fK(X,Y,Z)$; and $2g(
abla_X(fY),Z)=K(X,fY,Z)=fK(X,Y,Z)+2X(f)g(Y,Z)=2g(X(f)Y+f
abla_XY,Z)$ for all $Z$, so $
abla_X(fY)=X(f)Y+f
abla_XY$ by nondegeneracy.

Torsion vanishes. Subtracting the definitions of $K(X,Y,Z)$ and $K(Y,X,Z)$ and using symmetry of $g$ and skew-symmetry of the bracket cancels the $X,Y,Z$-derivative terms and the four bracket terms except $g([X,Y],Z)-g([Y,X],Z)=2g([X,Y],Z)$; hence $2g(
abla_XY-
abla_YX-[X,Y],Z)=K(X,Y,Z)-K(Y,X,Z)-2g([X,Y],Z)=0$ for all $Z$, and $T(X,Y)=
abla_XY-
abla_YX-[X,Y]=0$ by nondegeneracy.

Metric compatibility holds. Adding $K(X,Y,Z)$ and $K(X,Z,Y)$ cancels the $Y$- and $Z$-derivative terms by symmetry of $g$ and cancels the bracket terms by skew-symmetry, leaving $K(X,Y,Z)+K(X,Z,Y)=2X(g(Y,Z))$; dividing by two and using the defining property of $
abla$ gives $X(g(Y,Z))=g(
abla_XY,Z)+g(Y,
abla_XZ)$.

Any torsion-free $g$-compatible connection $
abla'$ satisfies $2g(
abla'_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$. Indeed, compatibility applied to the three pairings and torsion freedom written as $[X,Y]=
abla'_XY-
abla'_YX$, $[Z,X]=
abla'_ZX-
abla'_XZ$, $[Y,Z]=
abla'_YZ-
abla'_ZY$ turn the six terms of $K(X,Y,Z)$ into $
abla'$-terms in which $g(
abla'_XY,Z)$ occurs twice and every other term cancels in pairs. Hence $
abla'=
abla$ by the displayed defining property and nondegeneracy, proving claim (b) and the uniqueness assertion of (a).

In a chart, the brackets of coordinate fields vanish by [L2], so evaluating $K$ on coordinate fields with [L2] and [L4] gives $K(\partial_b,\partial_c,\partial_a)=\partial_bg_{ca}+\partial_cg_{ba}-\partial_ag_{bc}$; substituting $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_e\Gamma^e{}_{bc}\partial_e$ into step 3.1 gives $\sum_eg_{ea}\Gamma^e{}_{bc}=\tfrac12(\partial_bg_{ca}+\partial_cg_{ba}-\partial_ag_{bc})$ and multiplying by $g^{ad}$ gives the displayed Christoffel formula, whose right side is smooth by [L5].

(Dual and tensor components.) The dual connection of [L6] is a connection on $T^*M$, and its components are $(
abla^*_a\omega)_b=\partial_a\omega_b-\sum_d\Gamma^d{}_{ab}\omega_d$: with $\omega=\sum_b\omega_bdx^b$, the characterizing identity gives $(
abla^*_{\partial_a}\omega)(\partial_b)=\partial_a\omega_b-\omega(
abla_{\partial_a}\partial_b)=\partial_a\omega_b-\sum_d\Gamma^d{}_{ab}\omega_d$.

The product connection of [L6] extends $
abla$ and $
abla^*$ to all tensor bundles and satisfies the Leibniz rule on tensor products. Its two elementary values are $
abla_{\partial_c}\partial_b=\sum_d\Gamma^d{}_{bc}\partial_d$ and $
abla_{\partial_c}dx^a=-\sum_d\Gamma^a{}_{dc}dx^d$: the second follows from step 5.1 and $dx^a(\partial_b)=\delta^a{}_b$. Expanding a smooth tensor field $T$ in the coordinate product frame as $T=\sum T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}\,\partial_{a_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes dx^{b_1}\otimes\cdots$ and applying the Leibniz rule, exactly one $+\Gamma$ term appears for each upper slot and one $-\Gamma$ term for each lower slot, and the coefficient derivative $\partial_cT^{\cdots}$ appears once; this yields the displayed component formula, the sum over $d$ replacing the slot index.

The induced derivative commutes with contraction. Let $T$ be of type $(r,s)$ with $r,s\ge1$, contract one upper slot $a_i$ with one lower slot $b_j$, and contract the derivative in the same slots. The $+\Gamma$ term for the upper slot contributes $\sum_d\Gamma^{d}{}_{ec}T^{\cdots e\cdots}{}_{\cdots d\cdots}$ and the $-\Gamma$ term for the lower slot contributes $-\sum_d\Gamma^{e}{}_{dc}T^{\cdots d\cdots}{}_{\cdots e\cdots}$; relabelling the dummy indices $(d,e)\mapsto(e,d)$ in the second sum makes the two contributions equal and opposite, while the remaining terms are exactly the derivative of the contracted components by step 6.1. Summing over $d$ is a finite index sum, so both orders give the same smooth function.

The metric and inverse metric are annihilated. By step 6.1 with $T=g$, writing the two lower slots explicitly, $g_{ab;c}=\partial_cg_{ab}-\sum_d\Gamma^d{}_{ac}g_{db}-\sum_d\Gamma^d{}_{bc}g_{ad}=0$ by the compatibility identity of [L5]. Differentiating $g^{ad}g_{db}=\delta^a{}_b$ in the direction $\partial_c$ and substituting the compatibility identity gives $\partial_cg^{af}+\sum_d\Gamma^f{}_{dc}g^{ad}+\sum_d\Gamma^a{}_{dc}g^{df}=0$, which is $g^{af}{}_{;c}=0$ by step 6.1. This proves claim (c) and completes the proof.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and proof steps 3.1 and 6.1: On the empty base all local fields and tensor sections are empty; the uniquely defined connection is the empty operator. For (r,s)=(0,0) the tensor product is the scalar line and its covariant derivative is X(f).

Statement and proof steps 3.1 and 6.1: Nondegeneracy makes det(g_ab) nowhere zero. Local inverse construction and the matrix-inversion supplier require precisely this hypothesis. No inverse is asserted for a degenerate metric.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is not parametrized by an indexed family; uniqueness is proved in step 4.4 by evaluating an arbitrary candidate, so there is no length-one family case.

boundaries.evidence: Nondegeneracy is a hypothesis and its failure is the excluded boundary: step 2.1 identifies V by solving g(V,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)/2, which uses exactly that g_p is a nondegenerate bilinear form at each point; if g were degenerate the construction would not be available.

boundaries.reason: The result is pointwise and local: the Koszul form and the chart verification in steps 3.1 and 4.5 are evaluated at interior points of chart domains and no interval endpoints or boundary values are asserted.

boundaries.evidence: AC_omega for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure is explicit in the Statement. General tensor products are supplied by the canonical finite-product construction; Koszul inversion and local gluing require no further Choice.

boundaries.reason: The Statement asserts existence and uniqueness of a connection with two named properties and the extension of its derivative; it is not written as a biconditional, so no forward direction of an equivalence is claimed.

No reverse implication is claimed: the tensor-derivative clauses of steps 5.1, 6.1, 7.1 and 8.1 are constructions and identities, and the characterization of the connection by torsion freedom and compatibility belongs to the uniqueness argument of step 4.4, not to a converse stated in the item.

risk_review.notes: Checked all 12 steps and exact affine, bracket, inverse, tensor, dual/product and contraction suppliers. Koszul scalar rules give a local smooth covector and nondegeneracy patches the local fields uniquely; no positive-definiteness assumption is used in the calculation. Torsion and compatibility cancellations, Christoffel indices, both contracted-index cancellation and differentiated inverse identity are valid. Rank-zero tensor type means scalar derivative; empty M is vacuous. AC_omega is inherited, not arbitrary choice. Supplier definitions are Lorentzian in places, but the local inverse-matrix and component calculations explicitly prove the advertised general nondegenerate case.

citations.quote:
For a given connection on $E$ and a smooth curve on an interval with nonempty interior, the **covariant derivative along the curve** is
$$D_tV=(\gamma^*\nabla)_{\partial/\partial t}V.$$
Here $V$ is a section of the pullback bundle as in [[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]], and the pullback connection exists by [[thm-pullback-connection-is-well-defined-and-functorial]]. It is real-linear and satisfies $D_t(fV)=f'V+fD_tV$ for functions of the parameter.

At an included endpoint the smooth up-to-boundary coefficients have their one-sided derivative; equivalently any smooth local extension of the coefficients gives this value, because extensions agreeing on a one-sided interval have the same derivative there. For a piecewise smooth curve the derivative is defined on each piece, with separate one-sided derivatives at corners; those derivatives are not required to agree. A singleton interval carries no derivative operator under this convention and will have identity transport by definition. A zero section or a rank-zero bundle gives zero covariant derivative. Constant base curves can have sections with nonzero coefficient derivative.

The operator $D_t$ is independent of local frames. If $V=s\circ\gamma$ near a parameter value for an ambient local section $s$, then
$$D_tV=(\nabla s)_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t)).$$
Consequently any two such extensions give the same derivative. This is an agreement assertion when an ambient extension exists, not an assertion that every section along a curve extends.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.


**(d) Intrinsic construction before physical use.** For smooth local vector
fields define the Koszul expression

$$K(X,Y,Z):=Xg(Y,Z)+Yg(Z,X)-Zg(X,Y)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X).$$

Define $\nabla^g_XY$ by $2g(\nabla^g_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth local
$Z$. The proof below establishes existence, smoothness, the affine-connection
rules, metric compatibility, torsion freedom and uniqueness; it uses symmetry
and nondegeneracy, not positive definiteness. Thus $\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$
has this unique element, called the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$. The later
nondegenerate-metric theorem retains its fuller tensor-derivative statement.
Its Christoffel symbols in any chart are defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) and obey

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12 g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}),\qquad a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3.$$

**(e) Basic curvature and contractions.** The **curvature** of this connection
is the operator of [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]], with the fixed
sign convention

$$R^g(X,Y)Z:=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

The general affine-connection theorem
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]] proves that it depends pointwise
only on $X,Y,Z$ and is a smooth tensor. Define its chart components by
$R^g(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$.
Define the **Ricci tensor** and **scalar curvature** pointwise by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,w):=\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto R^g_p(z,w)v),\qquad S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\sharp_p\circ\operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p(v):=\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,\cdot).$$

Here $\sharp$ is the inverse metric isomorphism and traces are the
basis-independent trace of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Equivalently,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and
$S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, all sums from $0$ through $3$.
These are well-defined smooth fields by finite contraction of the smooth
components of $R^g$ and $g^{-1}$; basis independence follows from the trace
and the intrinsic maps just defined. No symmetry identity or field equation
is assumed here. Lowering the curvature output gives
$R_{abcd}=g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd}$, so the definitions agree with the full later
curvature item, which proves the remaining symmetries and coordinate formulas.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $\nabla$ be an affine connection on
$M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) and let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, with Christoffel symbols $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a
\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]])
and metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$. Then:

1. $\nabla$ is torsion-free ([[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]])
   if and only if $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\Gamma^a{}_{cb}$ for all $a,b,c$ in every
   smooth chart.
2. $\nabla$ is $g$-compatible ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) if and
   only if, in every smooth chart,

$$\partial_ag_{bc}=\sum_{d=0}^{3}\bigl(\Gamma^d{}_{ab}g_{dc}+\Gamma^d{}_{ac}g_{bd}\bigr) \qquad(a,b,c=0,1,2,3).$$

Thus $\nabla$ is metric-selected for $(M,g)$ if and only if both displayed
conditions hold in every smooth chart.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary with affine connection $\nabla$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. A smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ is an **affinely parametrized geodesic** when
$$D_t\gamma'(t)=0\qquad(t\in I),$$
with one-sided interpretation at an included endpoint. Constant curves are geodesics. Unless another parametrization is explicitly stated, “geodesic” means affinely parametrized geodesic.

For a piecewise smooth curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ and $v\in E_{\gamma(a)}$, let $V_v$ be the unique continuous piecewise parallel section with $V_v(a)=v$, supplied by [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-parallel-sections]]. Its **parallel transport** is
$$P_\gamma:E_{\gamma(a)}\to E_{\gamma(b)},\qquad P_\gamma(v)=V_v(b).$$
More generally, $P_{\gamma;s,t}$ sends initial data at $s$ to its value at $t$, allowing either order of the parameters. The same theorem gives independence from frames and subdivisions. On a singleton, $P_\gamma$ is the identity of its fibre. An empty curve has no endpoint fibres and is not assigned such a map. Zero initial data maps to zero; the transport depends on the supplied connection as well as the curve. Linearity and invertibility are proved next.

A section $V$ along a smooth curve is **parallel** if $D_tV=0$. By [[prop-local-frame-formula-for-covariant-differentiation-along-a-curve]], in a pulled-back frame this means
$$v'(t)=-\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))v(t).$$
For a piecewise smooth curve, parallel means continuous on the full parameter interval and parallel on each smooth piece. One-sided derivatives are used at the endpoints of a piece; no equality of the two derivatives at a corner is required. On a singleton, every prescribed fibre vector is a parallel section by convention; on an empty interval the empty section is parallel.

The zero section is parallel, and along a constant curve the coefficients in a constant fibre frame are constant precisely for parallel sections. The definition does not assert that all local coefficients in arbitrary moving frames are constant.

Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be smooth on an interval, with smooth one-sided data at included endpoints. For every $t_0\in I$ and $v_0\in E_{\gamma(t_0)}$ there is exactly one parallel section $V$ on all of $I$ with $V(t_0)=v_0$. The same holds for a piecewise smooth curve on a compact interval, with continuity at its finitely many corners. A singleton carries its prescribed vector. No AC is required for a supplied connection and curve.

For a given connection on $E$ and a smooth curve on an interval with nonempty interior, the **covariant derivative along the curve** is
$$D_tV=(\gamma^*\nabla)_{\partial/\partial t}V.$$
Here $V$ is a section of the pullback bundle as in [[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]], and the pullback connection exists by [[thm-pullback-connection-is-well-defined-and-functorial]]. It is real-linear and satisfies $D_t(fV)=f'V+fD_tV$ for functions of the parameter.

At an included endpoint the smooth up-to-boundary coefficients have their one-sided derivative; equivalently any smooth local extension of the coefficients gives this value, because extensions agreeing on a one-sided interval have the same derivative there. For a piecewise smooth curve the derivative is defined on each piece, with separate one-sided derivatives at corners; those derivatives are not required to agree. A singleton interval carries no derivative operator under this convention and will have identity transport by definition. A zero section or a rank-zero bundle gives zero covariant derivative. Constant base curves can have sections with nonzero coefficient derivative.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $c>0$ be a fixed real constant.
All curves below take values in $M$; the physical reading of $c$, of a
worldline as the history of a clock or body, and of the parameter values as
times is not part of this definition and is adopted separately in the
postulates of the framework.

**(a) Regularity classes.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A
**chart representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ for a smooth
chart $(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]).

- For $k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ and an interior point $t_0\in I$, the map
  $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ at $t_0$** when there is a chart representative
  $x\circ\gamma$ defined near $t_0$ that is $C^k$ there in the componentwise
  Euclidean sense. This condition is independent of the chart: on the overlap
  of two chart representatives the transition map is smooth and the chain rule
  applies ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]],
  [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). If $t_0\in I$ is an
  included endpoint of $I$, the coordinate representative and its derivatives through order $k$
  are continuous up to $t_0$ on the relative interval
  $I\cap(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$, with derivatives at
  $t_0$ taken one-sided. For $k=\infty$ this holds at every finite order.
  Merely possessing a one-sided secant tangent, as defined next, does not
  by itself make a curve $C^1$ at the endpoint. The map $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ on $I$** when it is $C^k$ at
  every point of $I$.

- Let $b\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. A curve
  $\gamma:(b-\varepsilon,b]\to M$ has **left tangent** $v\in T_{\gamma(b)}M$
  at $b$ when for one — equivalently every — chart $(U,x)$ around
  $\gamma(b)$, writing $v=\sum_{a=0}^{3}v^a\partial_a|_{\gamma(b)}$
  ([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the
  difference quotients satisfy
  $\bigl(x^a(\gamma(t))-x^a(\gamma(b))\bigr)/(t-b)\to v^a$ as $t\uparrow b$ for
  $a=0,1,2,3$. A **right tangent** at the left end of a curve is defined
  analogously with $t\downarrow b$. Chart independence is the one-sided
  chain-rule computation for the smooth transition maps
  ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

- A curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ is **piecewise $C^1$** when there is a
  finite partition $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ such that for every $i$ the
  restriction of $\gamma$ to $[s_{i-1},s_i]$ is $C^1$ up to its included
  endpoints in the one-sided sense above: in every endpoint chart its
  component derivatives on the open piece have continuous one-sided limits,
  agreeing with its endpoint derivatives. Equivalently each piece has a
  $C^1$ extension to its closed parameter piece. In particular its right
  tangent at $s_{i-1}$ and left tangent at $s_i$ exist. Such a
  partition is called **admissible** for $\gamma$. The piece extensions give continuity at the
  corners; no agreement of the
  two one-sided tangents at a corner is required.

**(b) Velocity.** If $\gamma$ is $C^1$ at an interior point $t$, its
**velocity** $\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation
$[f]\mapsto(f\circ\gamma)'(t)$ on smooth germs at $\gamma(t)$, extending
[[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]] from smooth to $C^1$ curves.
Equal germ representatives agree along the curve near $t$, and the
one-variable product rule proves the derivation identity. In a chart around
$\gamma(t)$ the velocity has the component
expression

$$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x^a\circ\gamma\bigr)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)},$$

the coordinate expression of the derivation
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). At an
included endpoint of the domain, $\gamma'$ means the corresponding one-sided
tangent of clause (a).

**(c) Timelike worldlines.** For $k\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$,
a **$C^k$ future timelike worldline** is a $C^k$
curve $\gamma:I\to M$ whose velocity $\gamma'(t)$ is future timelike at every
$t\in I$, in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]
and [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))<0$
and $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),N_{\gamma(t)})<0$. A **piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike worldline** is a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ whose
velocity at every point of each open piece and whose one-sided tangents at the
two ends of each piece are future timelike; the definition is applied to a map
on an arbitrary interval $I$ with nonempty interior by requiring it on every
compact subinterval of $I$. A future timelike velocity is in particular
nonzero, so every future timelike worldline is regular.

**(d) Proper time and length.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$
future timelike worldline and let $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ be an admissible
partition. On each open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the function
