$$h_i(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}\bigl(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s)\bigr)}$$

is continuous and strictly positive: it is a finite sum of products of
continuous real functions in any chart around a point of the piece, as
$g_{ab}\circ\gamma$ and the components of $\gamma'$ are continuous
([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and the
square root is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ ([[def-rational-power]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The continuous one-sided limits of the component derivatives, required
by the $C^1$ extension of each piece, and continuity of $g$ imply that
$h_i$ tends to the norm of the corresponding endpoint tangent. The future
timelike hypothesis on those tangents makes these limits strictly positive, and $h_i$ extends to a continuous function on
$[s_{i-1},s_i]$; hence it is Darboux integrable there
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). The
**proper-time increment** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is

$$\tau(b)-\tau(a):=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h_i(s)\,ds,$$

and the **Lorentzian length** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is
$L_g(\gamma):=c\,(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. For a base point $s_0\in I$ the
**proper-time function** $\tau:I\to\mathbb R$ of a future timelike worldline is
the function with $\tau(s_0)=0$ and $\tau(s)$ equal to the increment
from $s_0$ to $s$ when $s>s_0$, and minus the increment from $s$ to $s_0$
when $s<s_0$. That the increment is independent of the admissible
partition, so that $\tau$ is well defined, and that it is invariant under
increasing $C^1$ reparametrization are proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]; the display is the
value for any admissible partition.

**(e) Four-velocity.** Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike
worldline and let $t$ be a parameter value at which $\gamma$ is differentiable
(interior point of a piece, or an included endpoint with its one-sided
tangent). The **four-velocity** of $\gamma$ at $t$ is

$$U(t):=\frac{c\,\gamma'(t)}{\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M .$$

By construction $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$, and
$\gamma'(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}/c\bigr)U(t)$ with a strictly
positive scalar factor. If $U$ is written as the derivative of $\gamma$ with
respect to proper time, $U=d\gamma/d\tau$, this is a statement proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]], not part of the
present definition.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$c>0$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

1. **Well-definedness and additivity of proper time.** Let
   $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike worldline
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then the sum defining
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ is the same for every admissible partition of $[a,b]$; it
   is written $\frac1c\int_a^b h$, where $h$ is the piecewise-defined
   proper-time density. For every $u\in(a,b)$,
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)=\bigl(\tau(u)-\tau(a)\bigr)+\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(u)\bigr)$.
   If $a<b$, the increment is strictly positive.

2. **Reparametrization and orientation, including subintervals.** Let
   $a'<b'$ and let $\varphi:[a',b']\to[a,b]$ be $C^1$ up to its included
   endpoints with nonzero derivative everywhere, including one-sided endpoint
   derivatives. Let $\tilde\gamma:=\gamma\circ\varphi$. Its derivative has
   constant sign and $\varphi$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its actual image
   interval. If $\varphi'>0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline and
   $$\tilde\tau(b')-\tilde\tau(a')=\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a')).$$
   This equals $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ when $\varphi(a')=a$ and $\varphi(b')=b$.
   If $\varphi'<0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ **past** timelike
   traversal. Its unsigned density
   $\tilde h=\sqrt{-g(\tilde\gamma',\tilde\gamma')}$ obeys
   $$\frac1c\int_{a'}^{b'}\tilde h=\tau(\varphi(a'))-\tau(\varphi(b'))>0,$$
   whereas the oriented original difference
   $\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a'))$ is negative. For endpoint-reversing
   $\varphi(a')=b$, $\varphi(b')=a$, the latter equals
   $-\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(a)\bigr)$. This negative oriented difference is not
   elapsed proper time for a future curve; parameter reversal reverses the
   causal direction. Non-surjective maps compare increments over their
   actual image interval, not over the whole original interval.

3. **Proper-time function and four-velocity.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a
   $C^1$ future timelike worldline on an interval with nonempty interior and
   let $\tau$ be its proper-time function based at $t_0\in I$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then $\tau$ is $C^1$ on
   $I$ with
   $$\tau'(t)=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}>0,$$
   so $\tau$ is strictly increasing, and at every $t\in I$ the velocity,
   proper-time density and four-velocity satisfy
   $\gamma'(t)=\tau'(t)\,U(t)$ and $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$. If
   $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $I$ with image $J$, then the
   reparametrized curve $\gamma_\tau:=\gamma\circ(\tau|_I)^{-1}$ is a $C^1$
   future timelike worldline on $J$ with
   $$\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)=U\bigl(\tau^{-1}(\sigma)\bigr),\qquad g\bigl(\gamma_\tau'(\sigma),\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)\bigr)=-c^2 .$$
   The same formulas hold piece by piece for a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline, on each open piece and at its endpoints one-sided, with the two
   corner velocities kept distinct.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

derivations.claim: (Component form of $D_t$.) On a chart domain around a parameter value, let $e_a:=\partial_a\circ\gamma$ be the pulled-back coordinate frame and write $\gamma'=\sum_b\dot\gamma^be_b$, $V=\sum_aV^ae_a$, with coefficient functions $V^a$ on the parameter interval. By [L1], $D_te_c=(\nabla\partial_c)_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))=\sum_{a,b}\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\dot\gamma^be_a$. The pullback product rule therefore gives $D_tV=\sum_a\bigl(\partial_tV^a+\sum_{b,c}\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\dot\gamma^bV^c\bigr)e_a$. This uses ambient extensions only for the coordinate frame, not for the arbitrary coefficient functions along the curve, and hence also applies to repeated points and constant base curves. The same formula and pairing calculation hold for $C^1$ fields along a $C^1$ curve, with the derivatives interpreted at included endpoints one-sided.

(Metric pairing.) With the notation of step 1.1, $g(V,W)=\sum_{a,b}g_{ab}V^aW^b$, so $\frac{d}{dt}g(V,W)=\sum_{a,b}\bigl(\partial_cg_{ab}\dot\gamma^cV^aW^b+g_{ab}\partial_tV^aW^b+g_{ab}V^a\partial_tW^b\bigr)$. Substituting the compatibility identity of [L2] for $\partial_cg_{ab}$ and the component formula of step 1.1 for $D_tV$ and $D_tW$, the terms in which $\Gamma$ multiplies $V$ or $W$ match, using symmetry $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ and the relabelling of the summed indices $b,c,d$; the remaining terms are exactly the two derivatives $\partial_tV^aW^bg_{ab}$ and $V^a\partial_tW^bg_{ab}$. Hence the displayed pairing identity holds; if $D_tV=D_tW=0$, the derivative of the smooth function $g(V,W)$ vanishes on each chart, hence on $I$; [L7] gives constancy.

(Parallel transport.) On a singleton, [L4] and the transport definition give the unique prescribed vector and identity map, which preserves the metric. For $a<b$, let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be piecewise smooth and $v\in T_{\gamma(a)}M$. The existence and uniqueness of a continuous piecewise parallel section through $v$ is [L4]; the map $P_\gamma$ is therefore well defined, and it is linear because the difference of two parallel sections with initial values $v,w$ is a parallel section (linearity of $D_t$ from step 1.1) with initial value $v-w$. It is bijective with inverse given by the same construction for the reversed curve. For $v,w$ apply claim 1 to their parallel sections $V,W$ on each smooth piece: $g(V,W)$ has zero derivative there and is continuous across corners, hence constant on $[a,b]$ by [L7], so $g(P_\gamma v,P_\gamma w)=g(v,w)$.

(Constant speed and causal character.) Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic, so $D_s\gamma'=0$ by [L3]. Applying the pairing identity of step 2.1 with $V=W=\gamma'$ gives $\frac{d}{ds}g(\gamma',\gamma')=2g(D_s\gamma',\gamma')=0$ on every chart of the domain; hence $g(\gamma',\gamma')$ is a constant by [L7]. By [L4], the tangent $\gamma'$ is the parallel section with its value prescribed at any one parameter, and parallel transport is bijective. Thus if $\gamma'$ vanishes once it vanishes everywhere, so $\gamma$ is constant; otherwise it is nowhere zero. In the latter case its constant squared norm fixes its timelike, null or spacelike character on all of $I$. If it is causal, [L6] makes its continuous pairing with $N$ nowhere zero, so its time orientation is also constant, including the null case.

(Timelike geodesics and proper time.) Let $\gamma$ be a future-directed timelike geodesic with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-\lambda^2$, $\lambda>0$. Its proper-time density is $\sqrt{\lambda^2}/c=\lambda/c$, constant, so for $t_0<t_1$ the increment over $[t_0,t_1]$ is $\lambda(t_1-t_0)/c$ by [L5]; hence proper time is an affine function of the parameter and an affine parameter of $\gamma$. The four-velocity is $U=d\gamma/d\tau=(c/\lambda)\gamma'$; since $D_t\gamma'=0$ and $d\tau/dt=\lambda/c$ is constant, $D_\tau U=(c/\lambda)D_t((c/\lambda)\gamma')=0$. A nonconstant null geodesic has nonzero null tangent by step 3.2, so the integrand in [L5] is zero and the curve is not a future timelike worldline; it admits no proper-time parametrization.

(Affine reparametrizations.) Let $\gamma:I	o M$ have nowhere-zero tangent and be a geodesic; let $h:J	o I$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its open image with $h'
eq0$, and put $	ilde\gamma=\gamma\circ h$. In a chart and on each parameter interval where $h$ and $\gamma$ are taken on a fixed chart, $	ilde\gamma{}'=h'\,(\gamma'\circ h)$, so by step 1.1 $$D_s	ilde\gamma{}'=h''\,(\gamma'\circ h)+(h')^2\,(D_t\gamma')\circ h=h''\,(\gamma'\circ h),$$ where the last equality is the geodesic equation for $\gamma$ and the two terms arise exactly as in the product rule $D_s(h'\,(\gamma'\circ h))=h''(\gamma'\circ h)+h'\,D_s(\gamma'\circ h)$ with $D_s(\gamma'\circ h)=h'\,(D_t\gamma')\circ h$. Since $\gamma'\circ h$ is nowhere zero, $	ilde\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if $h''\equiv0$ on $J$, that is $h(s)=as+b$ with constants $a=h'
eq0$ and $b$. If $\gamma$ is constant, then $	ilde\gamma$ is constant and geodesic for every $h$ by [L3]. Conversely, every $C^2$ diffeomorphism with $h''=0$ has this affine form, and for a nonconstant geodesic starting from a fixed affine parameter $t$, every other affine parameter $s$ is related by $s=at+b$ with $a
eq0$ by applying the criterion to $h=s\circ t^{-1}$.

boundaries.reason: The Statement quantifies over each curve and each initial vector separately; existence and uniqueness of the parallel section are asserted for every prescribed v, so no empty-family vacuity arises.

boundaries.evidence: Derivative signs d/dt in step 2.1 and the reparametrization formula of step 5.1 carry no invertible-variable division that can fail: step 5.1 assumes h is a C^2 diffeomorphism with h'!=0, and the transport equation of step 3.1 is solved by Picard-Lindelof rather than by dividing by a coefficient.

boundaries.reason: There is no indexed family whose length-one case would be special: the claims are made for each curve, each geodesic and each initial vector individually.

boundaries.evidence: Statement explicitly requires nonempty interior for derivative domains I,J. Clause 2 separates singleton transport as the identity with no D_t condition; proof 3.1 verifies this branch. Nonconstant zero-norm tangents are null, zero tangents give constant curves, and lambda>0 is required for timelike normalization.

Statement clause 2 and proof steps 1.1 and 3.1: One-sided covariant derivatives are used on nondegenerate closed pieces; continuous pairing extends constants to endpoints and across corners. Singleton transport has no derivative operator.

Solutions are obtained from the cited existence-and-uniqueness theorem for parallel sections on each smooth piece and concatenated finitely many times in step 3.1; no selection from an infinite family is required beyond the inherited AC_omega of the ambient smooth structure.

The forward direction of claim 4 is step 5.1: assuming gamma is a geodesic and gamma-tilde=gamma circ h is a geodesic forces D_s gamma-tilde'=h''(gamma' circ h)=0, hence h''=0, and since h'!=0 the reparametrization is affine.

The reverse direction is also step 5.1: if h(s)=as+b with a!=0 then h''=0 and D_s gamma-tilde'=0, so gamma circ h is a geodesic, and applying the criterion to h=s circ t^{-1} shows every affine parameter of gamma arises from a fixed one.

risk_review.notes: Checked six steps: pullback-frame formula avoids assuming ambient extension for arbitrary along-curve sections, including repeated points. Compatibility gives pairing preservation; exact parallel-section existence supplier covers full intervals and finite corners. Reverse transport gives bijectivity and zero tangent forces a constant curve. Nonconstant null and spacelike cases distinguished from zero; future timelike norm lambda>0 gives affine proper time. Both directions of affine reparametrization use nowhere-zero tangent, with constant curves explicitly exempted. No additional choice or empirical conclusion.

citations.quote:
In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $V:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth. For
every $x_0\in U$ there exist $h>0$ and an open neighbourhood $W\subseteq U$ of
$x_0$ such that:

1. for every $y\in W$ there is a unique solution $\Phi(\,\cdot\,,y)$ of
   $x'=V(x)$ on $[-h,h]$ with $\Phi(0,y)=y$;
2. the map
   $$\Phi:(-h,h)\times W\to U,\qquad \Phi(t,y)=\Phi_t(y),$$
   is smooth in $y$ and $C^1$ in $t$, with
   $\partial_t\Phi(t,y)=V(\Phi(t,y))$ and $\Phi(0,y)=y$.

This is the local smooth flow of the autonomous vector field $V$.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time
interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every
$(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair
$(y,\lambda)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection; its existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Fix
$c>0$. All intervals $I,J$ below have nonempty interior. For a
smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ write $D_t$ for the covariant derivative along
$\gamma$ of [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]] with respect to
$\nabla$ (equivalently, the pullback of the Levi–Civita connection).

1. **Metric pairing.** For smooth sections $V,W$ of the pullback bundle
   $\gamma^*TM$,
   $$\frac{d}{dt}\,g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(V(t),W(t)\bigr)=g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(D_tV(t),W(t)\bigr)+g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(V(t),D_tW(t)\bigr).$$
   In particular, if $D_tV=D_tW=0$ on $I$, then $g(V,W)$ is constant on $I$.

2. **Parallel transport.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise smooth curve
   with $a<b$.
   For every $v\in T_{\gamma(a)}M$ there is exactly one continuous piecewise
   smooth section $V$ of $\gamma^*TM$ with $D_tV=0$ on each smooth piece and
   $V(a)=v$; the parallel-transport map
   $P_\gamma:T_{\gamma(a)}M\to T_{\gamma(b)}M$, $v\mapsto V(b)$, is linear,
   bijective, and satisfies
   $g_{\gamma(b)}(P_\gamma v,P_\gamma w)=g_{\gamma(a)}(v,w)$ for all $v,w$.
   For $a=b$, the unique section is its prescribed fibre vector and
   $P_\gamma$ is the identity; no $D_t$ condition is imposed on a singleton.

3. **Geodesic speed and proper time.** Along a geodesic
   $\gamma:I\to M$ ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]) the function
   $t\mapsto g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))$ is constant. If $\gamma$
   is nonconstant, its tangent is nowhere zero and its causal character
   (timelike, null or spacelike) is constant; a constant geodesic has zero
   tangent and is assigned none of those causal characters. If $\gamma$ is a
   **future-directed timelike geodesic** and
   $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-\lambda^2$ with $\lambda>0$, then for
   $t_0<t_1$ its proper-time increment over $[t_0,t_1]$ is
   $\lambda(t_1-t_0)/c$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]), so proper time is an
   affine parameter. In this parameter its four-velocity is
   $U=(c/\lambda)\gamma'$ and is parallel: $D_\tau U=0$. Proper time is not
   assigned to a past-directed curve by that definition; reversing the
   parameter gives a future-directed timelike geodesic with the same
   (positive) proper-time magnitude. A nonconstant null geodesic has null
   tangent and admits no proper-time parametrization.

4. **Affine reparametrizations.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a geodesic whose
   tangent is nowhere zero, and let $h:J\to I$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto
   its open image with $h'\neq0$. Then $\gamma\circ h$ is a geodesic if and
   only if $h(s)=as+b$ with constants $a\neq0$, $b$; in that case $a$ is the
   constant $h'$, and every affine parameter of this nonconstant geodesic
   arises in this way from a fixed one. If $\gamma$ is constant, then
   $\gamma\circ h$ is constant and hence geodesic for every such $h$; no
   affine restriction on $h$ follows.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary with affine connection $\nabla$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. A smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ is an **affinely parametrized geodesic** when
$$D_t\gamma'(t)=0\qquad(t\in I),$$
with one-sided interpretation at an included endpoint. Constant curves are geodesics. Unless another parametrization is explicitly stated, “geodesic” means affinely parametrized geodesic.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth and let $p\in M$. The **differential of $F$ at $p$** is the map $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ defined by
$$ dF_p(v)([g]):=v([g\circ F]) $$
for every derivation $v\in T_pM$ and every germ $[g]\in C_{F(p)}^\infty(N)$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$. Then there
is a real $\delta > 0$, a **Lebesgue number** for $\mathcal{U}$, such that every
nonempty $A \subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}(A) < \delta$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) satisfies $A \subseteq U$ for some
$U \in \mathcal{U}$.

Diameters of nonempty subsets of $X$ are defined because a compact space is
bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) and a subset of a bounded
set is bounded. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: (Chart geodesic system.) Fix a chart $(U,x)$; its domain is an open subset $x(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, so $D:=x(U)\times\mathbb R^4$ is open in $\mathbb R^8$, and the field $F(x,w)=\bigl(w,-\Gamma(x)[w,w]\bigr)$ is smooth on $D$ because the Christoffel symbols are smooth. By [L1], a smooth curve in $U$ is a geodesic exactly when its coordinate lift solves $\dot z=F(z)$. Conversely, every solution $z=(y,w)$ with values in $D$ satisfies $y'=w$ and $y''=-\Gamma(y)[y',y']$, so $x^{-1}\circ y$ is the corresponding geodesic.

(Local flow and joint smoothness.) By [L2], for every base state $z_0\in D$ there are $h>0$ and a neighborhood $Z$ of $z_0$ such that the local flow $\Phi:(-h,h)\times Z\to D$ is defined, solves the system, and is smooth in the state and $C^1$ in time with $\partial_t\Phi=F\circ\Phi$. The smooth-dependence conclusion of [L3] applies to the jointly smooth field $F$ on the common compact cylinder and gives that, for every finite order $m$, the derivatives of $\Phi$ of order at most $m$ in the state variable exist and are jointly continuous on $(-h,h)\times Z$; since $\partial_t\Phi=F\circ\Phi$ with $F$ smooth, induction on the total order (differentiating the identity in the state variables and using the jointly continuous lower-order derivatives) shows that all mixed derivatives of $\Phi$ exist and are continuous on $(-h,h)\times Z$. Hence $\Phi$ is smooth on its domain, and it is the unique local solution through every $y\in Z$.

(Agreement of solutions.) Let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ be geodesics whose parameter intervals share a nondegenerate interval $J$ containing a parameter $t_0$ with $\gamma_1(t_0)=\gamma_2(t_0)$ and $\gamma_1'(t_0)=\gamma_2'(t_0)$. Consider the set of $t\in J$ at which both their positions and tangent vectors agree. It is closed because the two lifted curves $t\mapsto(\gamma_i(t),\gamma_i'(t))$ in the Hausdorff tangent bundle are continuous. It is relatively open because, in a chart about any agreement point, the position--velocity lifts solve the same first-order system and local uniqueness from [L3] makes them agree nearby, including a one-sided neighborhood when that point is an included endpoint. It is nonempty by the data at $t_0$, so connectedness of $J$ makes it all of $J$. Applying this to each compact subinterval of the common domain proves agreement wherever both are defined. In particular two solutions through $(p,v)$ with the same value and tangent at parameter 0 agree on their common domain.

(Maximal geodesic.) Fix $(p,v)\in TM$ and let $\mathcal S$ be the set of all geodesics $\gamma$ defined on an open interval containing $0$ with $\gamma(0)=p$ and $\gamma'(0)=v$; it is nonempty by [L2] applied in a chart around $p$ to the state $(x(p),v)$, and its parameter domains all contain $0$. Let $I_{p,v}$ be the union of those domains and define $\gamma_{p,v}(t):=\gamma(t)$ for any $\gamma\in\mathcal S$ whose domain contains $t$; by step 2.1 this is independent of the choice of $\gamma$. The union of intervals containing $0$ is an interval containing $0$, and $I_{p,v}$ is open: if $t_0\in I_{p,v}$, then $t_0$ lies in the domain of some $\gamma\in\mathcal S$, and [L2] applied at the state of $\gamma$ at $t_0$ extends a representative solution to a neighbourhood of $t_0$ which, by step 2.1, agrees with $\gamma_{p,v}$ on the overlap. Every geodesic in $\mathcal S$ is a restriction of this union. To include arbitrary interval domains, let $\eta:J\to M$ be any geodesic with the same initial data, allowing included endpoints as in [[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]. At each included finite endpoint $e$ of $J$, smooth one-sided data give a position--velocity state $(\eta(e),\eta'(e))$. Step 1.2 gives a two-sided local solution through that state in a chart about $\eta(e)$; the one-sided coordinate lift of $\eta$ solves the same ODE, so uniqueness in [L3] makes them agree on their common one-sided interval. They therefore glue to a smooth geodesic across $e$. Opening the at most two included endpoints gives an extension $\widehat\eta$ on an open interval $\widehat J\supseteq J$ containing $0$, so $\widehat\eta\in\mathcal S$. Hence $J\subseteq I_{p,v}$ and $\eta=\gamma_{p,v}|_J$. In particular no extension on any strictly larger interval exists, whether open, closed or half-open, and any other maximal geodesic with the data equals this one. This proves (a).

(Smoothness of one geodesic.) For $\gamma=\gamma_{p,v}$ and $t_0\in I_{p,v}$, choose a chart around $\gamma(t_0)$ and apply step 1.2 at the state $(\gamma(t_0),\gamma'(t_0))$; the coordinate lift of $\gamma$ agrees near $t_0$ with the smooth local flow of that state, so $t\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $I_{p,v}$.

(Scaling.) Let $s\in\mathbb R$. For $s=0$, the constant curve at $p$ is a geodesic with initial data $(p,0)$ and is defined on all of $\mathbb R$ by [L4], so by step 3.1 it is $\gamma_{p,0}$, and $t\in I_{p,0}$ iff $0=0\cdot t\in I_{p,v}$ holds for all $t$, with equal values $p=\gamma_{p,v}(0)$. For $s\neq0$, put $J_s:=\{t:st\in I_{p,v}\}$. On $J_s$ the curve $t\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(st)$ is a geodesic with initial data $(p,sv)$: if $v\neq0$, its tangent is nowhere zero, since a geodesic whose tangent vanished once would, by uniqueness in step 2.1, be constant; then clause 4 of [L4] applies to the affine reparametrization $h(t)=st$. If $v=0$, the curve is constant and clause 4 of [L4] handles that case directly. The interval $J_s$ is maximal for these initial data: any geodesic extension on a strictly larger interval would, after the inverse affine change of parameter $t\mapsto t/s$, extend $\gamma_{p,v}$ beyond $I_{p,v}$, contrary to step 3.1. Thus uniqueness of the maximal geodesic in step 3.1 gives $J_s=I_{p,sv}$ and $\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$, proving (c).

(Openness and smooth dependence.) Let $t_0\in I_{p_0,v_0}$. If $t_0=0$, step 1.2 and the flow identity give smooth dependence near $(0,p_0,v_0)$. Otherwise let $K$ be the compact interval with endpoints $0,t_0$ and let $z:K\to TM$ be the position--velocity lift of $\gamma_{p_0,v_0}$. For every $s\in K$, step 1.2 supplies an open neighborhood $Z_s$ of $z(s)$ in a tangent-bundle chart and a local flow on $(-h_s,h_s)\times Z_s$ for some $h_s>0$. Compactness gives finitely many such neighborhoods $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m$ covering $z(K)$; their inverse images under $z$ form an open cover of $K$, so [L6] supplies a Lebesgue number $\delta>0$. Choose a partition of $K$ with mesh less than $\min(\delta,h_1,\ldots,h_m)$, traversed from $0$ toward $t_0$. Each subinterval then lies in some $z^{-1}(Z_i)$ and has length less than $h_i$, so its solution map is the corresponding local flow map. Compose these finitely many smooth maps; at each stage continuity lets us shrink the neighborhood of $(p_0,v_0)$ so the nearby state at the next node remains in the next selected flow neighborhood. Thus the position--velocity state at the last node depends smoothly on $(p,v)$ nearby, and a final local flow around $z(t_0)$ gives smoothness jointly in $(t,p,v)$ near $(t_0,p_0,v_0)$. This neighborhood is contained in $\mathcal G$, so $\mathcal G$ is open in $\mathbb R\times TM$ and the evaluation is smooth, proving (b).

(The exponential domain.) By (c), $1\in I_{p,sv}$ iff $s\in I_{p,v}$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$. Hence $\mathcal E_p=\{v:1\in I_{p,v}\}$ is the preimage of the open set $\mathcal G$ under the continuous map $v\mapsto(1,p,v)$, so it is open in $T_pM$; and if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $s\in I_{p,v}$ because $I_{p,v}$ is an interval containing $0$ and $1$, so $1\in I_{p,sv}$ and $sv\in\mathcal E_p$: the domain is star-shaped about $0$. The map $\exp_p$ is the restriction of the smooth evaluation of (b) to $\{1\}\times\{p\}\times\mathcal E_p$, hence is smooth, and $\exp_p(0)=\gamma_{p,0}(1)=p$.

(Differential at zero.) Choose a basis $e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$ with coordinate isomorphism $\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ and identify $T_0(T_pM)$ with $T_pM$ by the chart $\psi_p$. For $w\in T_pM$, the curve $t\mapsto\exp_p(tw)$ has, by (c), $\exp_p(tw)=\gamma_{p,tw}(1)=\gamma_{p,w}(t)$, so its velocity at $0$ is $\gamma_{p,w}'(0)=w$; hence $d(\exp_p)_0(w)=w$ for every $w$, that is $d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}$.

(Local diffeomorphism.) Since $d(\exp_p)_0$ is the identity, it is an isomorphism, so [L5] gives open neighborhoods $V\subseteq\mathcal E_p$ of $0$ and $U\subseteq M$ of $p$ such that $\exp_p|_V:V\to U$ is a diffeomorphism. Choose a Euclidean norm on the finite-dimensional space $T_pM$ and let $W_p$ be the open ball of some radius contained in $V$; it is open, contains $0$, is star-shaped, and $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto its open image. This proves (d) and completes the proof.

boundaries.reason: No aggregate family is quantified in the Statement; the domain of the maximal geodesic, the flow set and the exponential domain are defined from the initial-value problem for individual data (t,p,v).

boundaries.evidence: The zero-vector case is disposed of explicitly in step 4.2: for s=0 the constant curve at p is a geodesic with initial data (p,0), it is defined for all parameter values, and exp_p(0)=p in part (d).

boundaries.reason: The construction is not parametrized by a family size; the single geodesic through a data pair (p,v) is the object of the maximality claim of step 3.1, which is the theorem's content rather than a length-one boundary case.

boundaries.evidence: Degenerate initial data v=0 are included and handled: step 4.2 identifies the constant geodesic at p, and step 8.1 invokes the inverse function theorem only near 0 where d(exp_p)_0=id is invertible, so no claim is made where the differential degenerates.

The maximal domain is open. Proof 3.1 now opens every included finite endpoint of any competing geodesic by a two-sided local chart ODE solution through its one-sided position/velocity state, glued by IVP uniqueness. Thus maximality covers closed and half-open competitors, not only members of the initial open-domain family.

The maximal geodesic is obtained as the union of the chart-local solutions over the set of geodesic germs (step 3.1); the local steps invoke Picard-Lindelof with fixed constants and the flow-box chart of step 1.2, so the only selection is the inherited AC_omega of the smooth structure.

The forward direction of the scaling equivalence in claim (c) is step 4.2: for s!=0 the curve t -> gamma_{p,v}(st) is a geodesic with initial tangent sv at p, so t in I_{p,sv} gives st in I_{p,v} with gamma_{p,sv}(t)=gamma_{p,v}(st).

The reverse direction is the same identity read backwards in step 4.2: if st in I_{p,v} then gamma_{p,v}(st) is defined and equals gamma_{p,sv}(t), which places t in I_{p,sv}; the case s=0 is the constant curve disposed of separately.
